candidates.attacker_control: Anyone able to supply XML to the filter+xml input stream controls element and attribute names, the serialized parameter type via the default 't' attribute, and the nested XStream content. XMLInputFilterFactory always includes UnknownFilter in the generic input descriptor, which provides a generic block with a parameter suitable for reaching the parameter-unmarshalling code.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked for any XStream allowlist, addPermission, or setupDefaultSecurity call in the repository and found none; the only explicit security setup reference is the commented-out call in SafeXStream. ParameterXStream uses NoWarningXStream's custom unmarshal path rather than a restricted configuration. The sink requires an element-valued parameter under a recognized filter block, but the generic UnknownFilter descriptor supplies such a block. No builder annotation, type assignability check, or post-Class.forName validation was found. This does not prove a usable gadget exists or that a deployed endpoint exposes filter+xml.
candidates.impact: Server-side arbitrary object instantiation and field population from untrusted XML. With a suitable classpath gadget or side-effecting constructor/static initializer this can escalate to remote code execution in the XWiki server process; in weaker cases it can cause denial of service, class-loading side effects, or manipulation of filter processing. It also bypasses the declared parameter contract because the class is never checked against the expected type.
candidates.prerequisites: The deployed application must expose or internally pass untrusted XML to the filter+xml input converter (the HTTP/import endpoint is not present in this repository, so that wiring is unproven). A gadget class or a class whose initialization/instantiation has security-relevant side effects must be present on the server classpath for code execution; without one, the primitive still permits arbitrary class loading/instantiation and possible denial of service.
candidates.root_cause: The generic filter XML parser trusts a per-parameter XML attribute as a fully qualified Java class name and passes it directly to Class.forName, without checking assignability to the declared filter parameter type. The resulting class is then used as the root type for XStream unmarshalling. ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream do not configure an XStream allowlist or call the security setup, and the build pins XStream 1.4.17, so attacker-chosen classes can be initialized and populated from the nested XML.
candidates.title: Untrusted filter XML selects arbitrary XStream types
candidates.trace: XMLInputFilterFactory advertises filter+xml and adds UnknownFilter to its filter interfaces. DefaultXMLParser resolves a matching block and its parameter container, maps an indexed parameter element such as the first parameter to the declared descriptor parameter, and passes the DOM Element to unserializeParameter. If that element carries the configured type attribute (default 't'), DefaultXMLParser loads its value with Class.forName(..., true, contextClassLoader) and ignores the expected parameter type. XStreamParameterManager then invokes XStream.unmarshal, XMLTreeUnmarshaller starts conversion using that attacker-selected class, and ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream perform the conversion without an allowlist. The nested XML is therefore interpreted as XStream object state for the chosen class.
candidates.unverified: No code, tests, or payloads were executed. I did not verify an external HTTP/import entry point, the exact set of XStream converters available on a deployment classpath, or whether the pinned XStream release's built-in class checks would block every candidate class. The RCE impact is therefore conditional; the source-level unsafe type selection and unrestricted XStream configuration are directly evidenced.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data; CWE-470 Unsafe Reflection

coverage_summary: Reviewed the 1,409-file source snapshot using repository-wide literal searches and targeted source reads. Deeply inspected the filter XML/parameter parser and XStream code, XML/HTML cleaner and entity handling, extension serializer/repository code, Netflux/WebSocket endpoints, Velocity tools and introspection, crypto/PKIX, job status, classloader, environment, cache, and repository helpers. The P1 index covers 1,408 of 1,409 source files, with one file omitted and three parse errors; its 17,602 relations are syntax/navigation candidates only, with no control-flow, data-flow, or semantic resolution. No source files were excluded by size, sensitive path, or symlink filters; binary-like files would still be skipped by the text tools.
limitations: No build, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are source-level.
The filter+xml HTTP/import entry point and deployed classpath are outside this snapshot, so attacker reachability and gadget availability are unverified.
The relation index is partial and syntactic: 12,591 calls are unresolved, and one source file is not indexed; absence of a relation does not show absence of a call path.
The review focused on high-risk security sinks and did not exhaustively read every line of all 1,409 files or every XML/build configuration.
No external web, CVE, patch, or sibling-case data was consulted, per the assignment.

rejected_leads.lead: Netflux channel and history keys are generated with java.util.Random in Utils.getRandomHexString.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a plausible CWE-338 weakness for bearer channel keys and is directly network-facing, but I did not establish a practical PRNG-state recovery path or show that a predicted key grants a concrete cross-user action; the XStream type-injection path has a stronger direct sink and impact.

rejected_leads.lead: HTML restricted mode only converts script/style and XWikiHTML5TagProvider allows SVG without an attribute sanitizer.
rejected_leads.reason: Potentially enables XSS if the HTML cleaner is relied on as a security sanitizer, but the repository does not show a downstream untrusted-HTML-to-rendered-page sink or prove that SVG event attributes survive deployment configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultExtensionSerializer parses extension descriptors with a default DocumentBuilderFactory, enabling external entities.
rejected_leads.reason: The parser is unhardened, but its known callers load core or local extension descriptors from server-controlled files; I found no attacker-controlled descriptor ingestion path in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultJobStatusStore encodes job-id path elements with URLEncoder but leaves '..' unchanged, and XStream-based job/history readers are not allowlisted.
rejected_leads.reason: Could become a path traversal plus unsafe-deserialization chain, but the snapshot does not show attacker control of job IDs or a route to place a crafted status/history file at the traversed location.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtils.parse sets the disallow-doctype-decl parameter to false while its comment says it prevents XXE.
rejected_leads.reason: The three external-DTD/entity parameters are set to their safe false values, so this is mainly an internal-entity/DOCTYPE-hardening gap; I did not find a direct untrusted-source path where external entity expansion remains enabled.

rejected_leads.lead: Velocity exposes NIOTool, URLTool, and file/URL input-source helpers.
rejected_leads.reason: Dangerous primitives exist, but their exploitability depends on scripting rights, platform-specific Path conversion, and secure-introspection configuration not present in this repository.

summary: The strongest source-level lead is an unsafe deserialization path in the generic XML filter: an XML-supplied parameter type is loaded with Class.forName and handed to an XStream instance that has no type allowlist or security setup. The same parser always exposes the generic UnknownFilter event, so this is not dependent on application-specific filter parameters. Impact can include arbitrary object instantiation and field population, with server-side code execution if a usable classpath gadget/side-effecting class exists; otherwise denial of service or filter behavior manipulation. This is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
